newsitem.title: FRANCE: Guigou surprise choice for French justice minister.
newsitem.headline: Guigou surprise choice for French justice minister.

text.p: Elisabeth Guigou, a steely technocrat turned politician, was a surprise choice for the politically sensitive justice ministry in France's new Socialist-led government on Wednesday.

One of a number of Socialist women elected to the National Assembly in Sunday's general election, Guigou, 50, has built a career as an expert on the European Union and negotiated the Maastricht treaty as junior minister for European affairs.
But little in her background appears to prepare her for the delicate task of fulfilling the Socialists' campaign pledge to make the judiciary independent of political authorities at last.
Her predecessors on both left and right were often accused of interfering with the course of justice to block embarrassing investigations into corruption and illicit party funding.

Two major sleaze probes involving former centre-right ministers have been opened in the three days since last Sunday's parliamentary election, suggesting public prosecutors may have been ordered to block them until after the vote.

A longtime aide in the late president Francois Mitterrand's office, Guigou emerged from the shadows to defend the blueprint for a single European Union currency in a crucial 1992 referendum in which the treaty was approved by a narrow 51.05 percent.

A former Treasury technocrat specialised in the financial markets, she argued that France and most of its European partners had already lost monetary sovereignty to Germany but would recover a share of power with a single currency.

After years of backroom toil as an adviser to Mitterrand, the chic, sharp blonde was thrust into the limelight when he appointed her European affairs minister in October 1990, succeeding Edith Cresson.

A tireless worker for European integration and an able linguist with degrees in economics and American literature, she was credited by some commentators with keeping the door open to the hesitant British before Maastricht and believes in maintaining the special diversities of the continent's various parts.
"We are not going to plough under the centuries-old traditions of Britain, France and other countries of European Community to transform them into Dakota and Kansas," she said.
But she stood fast on France's commitment to a social welfare element to the union accord.
"We don't want just a Europe of travelling salesmen, a big free trade zone," she said at Maastricht.
The daughter of a French farmer in Morocco, she was born outside the charmed circle of the French political elite.

But marriage at 19 to Socialist economist Jean-Louis Guigou, now head of France's regional development authority (DATAR), and a place at the prestigious Ecole Nationale d'Administration (ENA) civil service college set her on course for a glittering Treasury career.
In 1982 she was plucked from the London embassy, where she was finance attache, by then-finance minister Jacques Delors who appointed her to his personal office.
But she was almost immediately poached by Mitterrand, who made her his personal economic adviser at the age of 38.

Her long association with the Socialist cause did not stop her working with then-conservative prime minister Jacques Chirac during the period of his "cohabitation" with Mitterrand in 1986-88, which commentators say marked her as a pragmatist.
Guigou has often seemed more at ease as a negotiator than in public. Her television appearances are often cold and she lacks the common touch to appeal to voters.
Born Elisabeth Vallier at Marrakesh on August 6, 1946, she married Jean-Louis Guigou in 1966. They have a son. 041848 GMT jun 97
